# Linkage and crossing over

## 1. Introduction
Opening frame for **Linkage and crossing over** — what the topic is, why it matters, a real-world hook (Nepal where possible), the map of what follows, and the learning outcomes (biology-plan.md §3.1, block I). Prose depth is written in the Heredity and Evolution fill pass.

## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Linkage and crossing over

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

Mendel's second law assumes genes assort independently — but genes live on chromosomes, and a chromosome carries hundreds of them. Genes on the **same chromosome** tend to be inherited together: this is **linkage**, and it was proved by T. H. Morgan's work on *Drosophila* (1910–1915). During prophase I of meiosis, homologous chromosomes swap segments at chiasmata — **crossing over** — which breaks linkage apart in proportion to the distance between the genes. Recombination frequency became the ruler of the genetic map.

## 3. Classified tables

Tables carry examples in every classification and characteristics row, ≤ 12 rows, and each is referenced from the body text (§3.3).

**Concept flow — from Mendel's exception to the genetic map (study in this order)**

| Step | Concept | Who / when | Key result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Chromosomes carry Mendel's factors | Sutton & Boveri, 1902–03 | Gene behaviour parallels chromosome behaviour |
| 2 | Two genes on one chromosome stay together | Bateson & Punnett (sweet pea) | Deviations from 9:3:3:1 toward parental types |
| 3 | Sex-linkage proves genes ride on chromosomes | Morgan, white-eyed fly, 1910 | Eye colour inherited with sex |
| 4 | Complete linkage — no recombination | Morgan's mutant strains | Only parental gametes |
| 5 | Crossing over at chiasma in prophase I | Cytology of meiosis | Recombinant gametes appear |
| 6 | Recombination frequency ∝ distance | Sturtevant, 1913 | First genetic map, 6 loci on the X chromosome |
| 7 | 1% recombination = 1 map unit (centimorgan) | Modern usage | Map distance, not physical distance |

**Complete vs incomplete linkage — classified comparison**

| Feature | Complete linkage | Incomplete linkage |
|---|---|---|
| Crossing over | Does not occur between the genes | Occurs between them at a chiasma |
| Gamete types | Only 2 parental types (AB, ab) | All 4: parental (AB, ab) + recombinant (Ab, aB) |
| Recombinant frequency | 0% | Between 0% and 50% |
| F₂ ratio | Not 9:3:3:1 — only parental phenotypes | 9:3:3:1 distorted toward parental classes |
| Distance between genes | Very close on the chromosome | Far enough apart for a chiasma in between |
| Example | Genes inside a Y chromosome or pericentric inversion | Most autosomal gene pairs in Drosophila |

**Coupling vs repulsion phase — how the alleles sit on the chromosomes**

| Feature | Coupling (cis) | Repulsion (trans) |
|---|---|---|
| Arrangement | Dominant alleles on one homologue: AB / ab | Dominant alleles on different homologues: Ab / aB |
| Parental gametes | AB and ab | Ab and aB |
| Recombinant gametes | Ab and aB | AB and ab |
| Test-cross offspring | Mostly round-yellow and wrinkled-green | Mostly round-green and wrinkled-yellow |
| How to tell them apart | Phenotypes of the most frequent progeny | Same rule — the frequent classes are the parentals |

## 5. Worked examples and applications
≥ 6 worked examples with solved steps, live examples and Nepal-context applications (biology-plan.md §3.1, block V) — written in the unit fill pass.

## 6. Key terms and statements
Every new term defined once; exam-grade definitions live here and in keyPoints (block VI).

**Worked example.** A test cross of a female *Drosophila* heterozygous for b (black body) and vg (vestigial wings) gives: b+vg+ 860, b vg 880, b+ vg 45, b vg+ 40. The two large classes are the parentals; the two small classes are recombinants. Recombination frequency = (45 + 40) / 1825 ≈ **4.7%**, so b and vg are about **4.7 map units** apart. The farther apart two genes are, the more often a chiasma falls between them — up to a maximum of 50 cM, where the genes behave as if unlinked.

## 7. Exam Zone
NEB past-question map (long/short), topic-wise MCQs with explanations, and short tricks (block VII). Existing entrance-exam (CEE) material stays where it is; this zone grows around it — see the seeded exam fields of this file when present.

**Most-asked points (NEB).** (1) Define linkage and crossing over and state where and when crossing over happens (pachytene of prophase I, at chiasmata). (2) Why does linkage violate the 9:3:3:1 ratio? (3) Calculate map distance from test-cross data. (4) Distinguish coupling from repulsion phase. (5) State the chromosome theory of inheritance and how Morgan's white-eyed male supported it.

## 8. Summary and self-check
5–10 line chapter summary, self-check questions and the common-confusions list (block VIII) — completed in the unit fill pass.

**Summary.** Genes on the same chromosome are linked; crossing over in prophase I breaks the linkage in proportion to distance, and the recombination percentage is the map distance in centimorgans. Linkage is the great exception to independent assortment — and the tool that let Sturtevant draw the first chromosome map. **Self-check:** from a test-cross table, can you spot the parentals, count the recombinants and compute the cM distance?

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Linkage: genes on the SAME chromosome tend to inherit together, violating independent assortment; coupling phase (AB/ab) vs repulsion (Ab/aB).
Trick 2: Crossing over in pachytene of prophase-I produces recombinants; recombination frequency ∝ distance between genes (1 map unit = 1% recombination).
Trick 3: Strongly linked genes (close together) show FEWER recombinants; a test cross ratio near 1:1:1:1 means unlinked genes — read the data this way.
Trick 4: Significance: crossing over creates variation for evolution; linkage preserves favourable gene combinations.
